Market 40 Script

LINK: This year marks the 40th anniversary of June 16th - the day thousands of young black people marched for their liberation. It also marks the 40 anniversary of the Market Theatre, an iconic space where the story of the South African struggle played out. If ever a place could be called ‘the peoples theatre, this is it.

James: There couldn’t be another peoples theatre but the market theatre. I’ve now been working as an artistic director for 2 years in my travels around the world, talking to people it is very clear that the market theatre is viewed as the National Theatre of SA

LINK: The Market theatre might not actually have happened but for a chance phone call by a city engineer to a young theatre entrepreneur.

Mannie: And he said, I’ve have a crazy idea, His idea was that there was this round building which was then the Indian fruit market, and he said I think this place could be a theatre.


When Mannie Manim stepped into the bustling fruit market for the first time, he immediately recognized it’s potential for what it is today

Mannie: Everybody who was close to me would say, have you lost your mind? Do you know what you are doing? Here I was coming to a deserted market building where there was nobody and nothing.

Bongani: So what was the vision?

Mannie: So the vision was theatre by all South Africans, for all South Afircans”

Through a kink in the law, the market theatre was able to accommodate blacks and whites despite the group areas act. As a commercial space for Indian traders the market theatre building was one of the few under apartheid, which was zoned for all races

Mannie: If we dreamt of a location for our dream theatre, we couldn’t have dreamt of a better place.

Mannie and his business partner Barney Simon rolled up their sleeves, and with capital from their pensions of just R6000 began the conversion

John: It looked like and explosion had taken place. It was like concrete all over. And Mannie and Barney said, there is going to be a stage, here we are going to do a circle seating like the Globe, here is going to be a little gallery, thus began my relationships with the Market theatre with these two white dudes.

From the start, it was a non-racial collective, with actors stepping in to renovate, scrape and paint

Benji: I was in charge of what we called volunteer labour and I must say it was a wonderful thing to see so many actors coming and giving their time.

Mannie: for instance, the upstairs theatre was built virtually entirely by the actors.

The main theatre opened with a production of the Marat Sade on June 19th.

Mannie: The opening song is we want the revolution now. And it said everything we wanted to say.

In the days running up to the opening performance there was a real revolution building in the wings

Sandra: it was terribly exciting, it was… Cause it was so real there was so much going on in the streets, with people protesting, busses burning and the play being about revolutions was incredibly exciting

Sandra Prinsloo played Charlotte Corday in the Marat Sade.
The invited audience of dignitaries and officials were outraged by the Market’s first offering.

Mannie: And after 10 minutes they were leaving already.

Throughout the performance, the theatre slowly emptied out

Mannie: And then I started saying, ‘That’s right, leave! We don’t want you here anyway!”

(music)

The Market Theatre had their first run in with the law with the musical production of The Me Nobody Knows.

Benji: The Me Nobody Knows was the first integrated production at The Market, it was also the first musical at the market.

It piqued the interest of security police, with images of it’s black and white cast on publicity posters.

Benji: Part of my brief was to encourage black participation at The Market. Those times were difficult times. Our people couldn’t just come from the townships here


Benji Frances directed the production of the Me Nobody Knows.
The mixed race cast and audiences were a flagrant dismissal of the group areas act.

Vanessa: We carried on, they couldn’t really do anything about it, unless they were to rewrite the law, which would have affected businesses all over and would have affected white people.

Actress Vanessa Cook was a founding member of the market theatre company.

Vanessa: We became quite rebellious immediately and always did what we wanted to do after that

John: I think we were foolhardy Bongani, we were just, I don’t know, there was a fire and a passion and a wanting to do the things that we believed were right.

In collaboration with Winston Ntshona and Athol Fugard, John brought a new South African voice to the market theatre.

John: Island made young white people ask – what kind of justification can we give to our children – why is Mandela kept there if we’re asking for a normal society?

LINK: The works coming out of the Market Theatre become known as the living newspaper. Plays like Woza Albert, Bopha, Sizwe Banzi is dead travelled the world with an eloquent message in opposition to the apartheid governments atrocities

The Market Theatre inadvertently created it’s own brand of theatre - dubbed protest theatre by disapproving authorities of the time

(upsounds)

John: It was a time in 1985 when the government went wild to silence all forms of protest

Surprisingly it was a Swedish classic, Miss Julie, written in the 1800’s that caused the biggest stir.

Sandra: Well you know Miss Julie is about an upper class young woman who falls in love with someone who is a gardener or worker for her father. And that was absolutely forbidden

Sandra Prinsloo leapt at the chance to play Miss Julie opposite John Kani

John: What’s wonderful about this character is that he’s being seduced by the madam

Sandra: Seducing John … It didn’t take much to seduce him.

John: I put my hand on the side of her body, and I could hear me breath in the audience. By the time I touched her breast there was “uhhh nee foc – dis darrim genoeg”

That kiss set off hate mail and bomb threats and also excited a strong response from hallowed halls

John: Dr Treunicht held the picture in parliament and said “So sal die toekoms lyk as ons nie versigtig nie. Die man is n terrorist”

The 80’s ushered in a violent state of emergency in an attempt to quell heightened resistance across the country

Bongani: Townships on fire, PW Botha – how did you navigate all of that?

Mannie: Our artists were responding, so Mboneni – Sarafina. One morning I’m sitting in my office, I hear a piano and there were beautiful voices and he brought the beginning of the cast of Serafina into the foyer.

In 1987 the musical Sarafina opened at the Market and became the biggest and most successful musical to be produced in Africa. It played at the Lincoln theatre in NY, ran on Broadway for 8 years and toured the world with it’s call for Freedom....

Mannie: And having that play on the stage was the most wonderful affirmation, we felt alive.

... and Freedom came in the 90’s with the release of Mandela and the first democratic elections.

John: It was incredible for instance in 1990 when Nelson Mandela was released. It was a commotion in the arts world. We had written about 300 plays – release Nelson Mandela which had to be shredded because he’s now in Soweto

International donor funding for the market theatre project dried up, actors, directors and management alike had to find a new way forward.

John: And it was a very trying time because we had to sit together, Barney Mannie and myself and there was Vanessa Cook, sat and said, ‘what are we going to do now? What is the Market Theatre voice going to be?”

They came up with a commitment to be a place of excellence, and handed the baton over to new generation of actors and directors.
The current artistic director James Ngcobo believes the market theatre has found a new voice.

James: We getting to a space where we are bravely evolving the space to say we do everything at the Market. That entertainment is not a swear word at the Market theatre.

They showcase homegrown South African music… new voices in film and contemporary dance.

James: People now know that they can come to watch dance.

The market theatre is rooted in it’s legacy and is always driven by a commitment to be local, to be relevant and to reflect the real world it lives in.
